chunks.text: How-to · May 23, twenty twenty-six · 8 min read · By Don Goldstein

A twenty twenty-six Uberall study found 83% of restaurants never surface when a diner asks an AI assistant for a recommendation, even though 86% have a Google listing. The gap comes down to four numbers you can check this week.
In short
AI assistants name only three to five restaurants per query, a twenty twenty-six Uberall study found 83% of restaurants never make that list, despite 86% having a Google profile.
Four numbers decide it: your star rating against the assistant floors, review recency, profile completeness, and whether your site holds an answer the AI can quote.
The rating floors run about 4.3 for ChatGPT, 4.1 for Perplexity, and 3.9 for Gemini, below the floor, rank and completeness do not save you.
Read all four this week in about ten minutes, then close the nearest gap first.

Ask your phone, out loud, for a good taco place near you. You will hear three names. Maybe five. Not ten blue links, not a map with twenty pins, three names, summarized at the top of the answer. If your restaurant is not one of them, the diner never learns you exist, and your position on the old Google map never gets read.

This is the part operators miss. A twenty twenty-six Uberall study of multi-location restaurants found that 83% never appear in AI search results, even though 86% of them keep a Google Business Profile . Having the listing is not the same as being named. The assistant has already decided who makes the shortlist before ranking ever enters the picture.

The invisibility gap. Eighty-six percent of multi-location restaurants keep an active Google Business Profile. Eighty-three percent of those same restaurants are invisible in AI search, never named when a diner asks an assistant for a recommendation. The two columns sit nearly side by side, almost the same height, showing how presence and inclusion have come apart: keeping the listing no longer gets you into the answer.
You do not need a consultant to find out which side of that 83% you are on. Four numbers decide it, and you can read all four this week.
Why presence stopped being enough.

When a diner asks ChatGPT, Gemini, or Google’s AI Overview for a recommendation, the assistant does not return a ranked list of everyone nearby. It returns a written answer that names three to five places. Uberall measured the shortlist at three to five brands per query. Everyone else is not on page two, they are simply not in the sentence.

What each discovery surface returns, side by side. The first ring shows three to five names, the size of the shortlist an AI assistant reads out per query. The middle ring shows about ten, the map pack snapshot a diner skims before scrolling. The third ring shows twenty or more, the number of restaurants in a single neighborhood that might have surfaced on an old pinned map. The named set shrinks dramatically the closer the surface gets to the diner's ear.

So the goal moved. Ranking first in the map pack still matters, but it no longer guarantees the assistant repeats your name. The assistant filters on a handful of signals first, then writes. Four of those signals are numbers you control.
Number one, your rating against the floor.

Each assistant appears to apply a minimum star rating before it will name a place at all. Uberall’s twenty twenty-six figures put the floors at roughly 4.3 for ChatGPT, 4.1 for Perplexity, and 3.9 for Gemini . Below the floor, completeness and rank do not save you, you are filtered out before the assistant starts choosing.

The move is not “get more stars.” It is to know your current number and the gap to the nearest floor. A restaurant sitting at 4.0 is invisible to ChatGPT’s shortlist no matter how good the food is; the same restaurant clears Gemini’s 3.9 today. Pull your number, write down the gap, and you know exactly which assistant you are losing. The G B P grader reads it for you if you would rather not do the arithmetic by hand.

Minimum star rating to be named by each AI assistant, on a scale from three point five stars to four point five stars. ChatGPT will not name a restaurant under about four point three stars. Perplexity's floor is about four point one. Gemini's is about three point nine. Floors are Uberall's twenty twenty-six reported figures. A restaurant sitting at four point zero clears Gemini's floor but falls below both Perplexity and ChatGPT.
Number two, review recency, not just the count.

A 4.6 built on twelve reviews, the newest from eighteen months ago, reads as a closed restaurant to a model trained to weight freshness. A 4.4 with a handful of reviews this month reads as open, busy, and current. Count earns the attention; recency keeps it.

The lever here is review responsiveness, fresh reviews arrive faster when you are visibly answering the ones you already have. The full playbook is in how to respond to Google reviews ; the short version is that a reply is a dated signal of life, and the assistant can read the date.
Number three, how complete the profile actually is.

86% have a profile. Far fewer have a profile the assistant can actually read. A listing with no hours-by-day, no cuisine set, no service attributes, and no menu link is a thin signal, the model has nothing to quote when the diner asks “are they open Sunday” or “do they do gluten-free.” Presence, again, is not the same as legibility.

Fill the structured fields on your Google Business Profile the way you fill out a permit: every field, no blanks, current. Hours by day, cuisine, dietary attributes, outdoor seating, the link to your real menu. The G B P grader flags the empty fields; the S E O grader checks whether your own site backs them up.
Number four, do you own an answer the AI can lift?

The assistant needs a sentence to quote. If the answer to “is it good for a group of eight,” “is there a vegan entrée,” or “can you book a patio table” lives only inside a photographed menu or a P D F, the model cannot lift it, it quotes a competitor who wrote the answer in plain text. The restaurants that get named are the ones that put the answer where a machine can read it.

That means text on your own pages plus restaurant schema markup so the structured facts are unambiguous. Run schema check to confirm the markup parses. This is the one number that lives on your site rather than your Google listing, and it is the one most operators have never looked at.
The fixes that backfire.

Two reflexes make the numbers worse. Buying reviews spikes the count and then tanks recency the moment the batch ages, and Google’s filters increasingly strip them, so the average drops and the dates go stale at once. Stuffing keywords into your business name is a suspension risk that can pull the whole listing, taking all four numbers to zero in a day. The signals that move AI search are the slow, real ones: good food showing up as fresh reviews, a complete profile, and answers written in plain text.
The ten-minute version.
You do not have to fix all four today. You have to read all four today, so you know which one is costing you.

The fourth number is the one that decides number four, so it is worth seeing the difference up close. Here is the same fact, “can you seat a group of eight on the patio”, written two ways. The first is how most restaurants ship it; the second is what the model can actually quote.

A before-and-after of the same restaurant fact, written two ways, showing why number four decides whether an AI assistant can name you. The before version is an image: a photographed menu card that reads, in a script font, large parties welcome on the terrace. A human can read it; the model sees only an image file with no extractable text, so when a diner asks whether you seat a group of eight on the patio, the assistant has nothing to lift and quotes a competitor who wrote the answer in plain text. The after version is plain text on the restaurant's own page under a clearly worded heading: yes, our covered patio seats groups up to twelve, and we hold patio tables for parties of six or more with a reservation. Same fact, but now it is machine-readable, so the assistant can quote it directly and name the restaurant in the answer. The lesson: the answer has to live as text the model can lift, not as a picture only a person can read.

Four numbers, ten minutes, no agency. The 83% are not invisible because AI search is unfair to small restaurants. They are invisible because no one has read these four numbers and closed the nearest gap.
Key takeaways
Presence is not inclusion, a Google listing does not mean an AI assistant will name you.
A restaurant below an assistant's rating floor is filtered out before ranking ever applies.
Review recency reads as proof of life; a dated reply is a signal the model can see.
Structured Google Business Profile fields are what the assistant quotes, blank fields read as silence.
The answer a diner asks for has to live in text on your own site, or a competitor's text gets quoted instead.
